Q: JSON, Jackson and multiline string A:

If you activate these features:

  • JsonReadFeature.ALLOW_BACKSLASH_ESCAPING_ANY_CHARACTER

  • JsonReadFeature.ALLOW_UNESCAPED_CONTROL_CHARS

the following JSON will work:

{ "content" : "A\
B\
C" }

If you use the .json5 extension then also editors should understand this construct.

Q: Is there a more succinct way to convert a String to a Set of Characters in Java? A:

tl;dr

No need to define your hexadecimal digits. If your goal is merely validating text input as hexadecimal digits, write a one-liner to check that each code point represents a hexadecimal base-16 digit by passing 16 to Character.digit.

boolean allHexDigits = 
    inputString
        .codePoints()
        .allMatch( codePoint -> 
            Character.digit( codePoint , 16 ) >= 0  // Test if code point represents a character that is a hexadecimal (Base 16) digit. 
        ) ;

Or if you insist on using char type, use solution from Comment by Venkata Raju:

boolean isHexDigit = ( ch <= 'f' ) && ( Character.digit( myChar , 16 ) >= 0 ) ;

Avoid char

Beware: The char type (and its wrapper class Character) has been essentially broken since Java 2, and legacy since Java 5. As a 16-bit value, char is physically incapable of representing most characters.

The char type does work in your particular case but only because your characters happen to come from the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), the first 64K characters in Unicode. But one emoji could ruin your day.

Code points

Instead of char, use code point integer numbers when working with individual characters. Every one of the 159,801 characters defined in Unicode has been permanently assigned a code point number in the range of 0 to 1,114,111.

You can easily generate an IntStream of code points for the characters in a string. From there map each code point back to text, text containing a single character. Collect into a list.

List < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .toList() ;

You asked for an unmodifiable Set. Just use Set.copyOf for that in Java 10+.

Set < String > hexDigitsSet = Set.copyOf( hexDigits );

A Set has no promise of any particular order, and indeed the order may even change between iterations. If you want those characters kept in your original order, use a SequencedSet in Java 21+. Choose a concrete class such as LinkedHashSet to preserve insertion-order.

SequencedSet < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( LinkedHashSet :: new )
        );

Or, perhaps you want those characters kept in alphabetical order. Use a concrete class such as TreeSet for natural-order.

SequencedSet < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( TreeSet :: new )
        );

You can make either SequencedSet unmodifiable.

SequencedSet < String > unmodifiableHexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableSequencedSet( hexDigits ) ;

Mark as final to avoid re-assignment of the reference.

final SequencedSet < String > unmodifiableHexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableSequencedSet( hexDigits ) ;

Caveat

Be aware that the approach described here only works for simple text such as seen in your Question.

Some of what you might perceive as single characters in some text is actually composed of multiple code points. For example, diacriticals (accent marks), and modified emoji (skin tones, etc.).

Earlier Java

Sequenced Collections arrived in Java 21, including SequencedSet. See JEP 431 and talk by Stuart Marks.

For earlier Java, you are limited to these more general interfaces:

Order Class Interfaces before Java 21 Added in Java 21+
Insertion-order LinkedHashSet Set, Collection SequencedSet, SequencedCollection
Natural-order or Comparator TreeSet SortedSet, NavigableSet, Set, Collection SequencedSet, SequencedCollection

Here is example code for Java 9 and later.

NavigableSet < String > hexDigits =                             // Java 6+. 
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()                                           // Java 9+.
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( TreeSet :: new )           // Java 8+.
        );
hexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableNavigableSet( hexDigits );  // Java 8+.

Q: How can I automatically rotate a UniFi (UDM Pro) Wi‑Fi password monthly and push the new password to devices without manual re‑entry? A:

Is there any way for the new password to automatically sync to all connected devices so that users don’t have to manually enter the updated password each month?

No – and that would kind of defeat the point of rotating the password. The controller cannot distinguish between "legitimate" devices and "illegitimate" ones. If there were such a password sync feature, then it would sync the new password to all devices which know the old one – even the ones which aren't supposed to know it (i.e. the ones that the password change is supposed to be protecting from).

If this isn’t possible with WPA2/WPA3 Personal, is there another UniFi‑supported approach (e.g., WPA2‑Enterprise + RADIUS, certificates, UniFi Identity Enterprise, NPS, etc.) that would allow password rotation without requiring users to update their Wi‑Fi settings?

WPA-Enterprise makes password rotation unnecessary in the first place, as there is no single shared password anymore, only individual device certificates (or, at minimum, individual user passwords) which are not shared/published, and therefore more easily revoked one-by-one.

Q: Multithreading Programs A:

“Async” operations are just a more modern and hopefully easier method to control multiple threads. Under the hood it is all multithreading.

Q: Accessing hidden member through derived instance selects base class member A:

It's a bit weird thinking about how to address this kind of question. The C# specification talks about what the new modifier does:

A class-member-declaration is permitted to declare a member with the same name or signature as an inherited member. When this occurs, the derived class member is said to hide the base class member. Hiding an inherited member is not considered an error, but it does cause the compiler to issue a warning. To suppress the warning, the declaration of the derived class member can include a new modifier to indicate that the derived member is intended to hide the base member.

That is, the only effect of the modifier is to remove a compiler warning. It doesn't affect anything else, so it's completely irrelevant to what you're asking. In fact, it's another way in which the AI answer is entirely wrong, because hiding has nothing to do with the new modifier in C#.

So what we actually want to look at is how members are resolved in C#. If I have a public member on a base class, and a private member with the same name (and arguments for methods) in a derived class, will the private member hide the public member? Let's look at what the specification says about member hiding (§10.7.1.2):

A constant, field, property, event, or type introduced in a class or struct hides all base class members with the same name.

So properties are hidden based on their name. But whether a member hides another member or not depends on the scope!

A declaration of a new member hides an inherited member only within the scope of the new member.

Since you're looking from the outside, the private member is not within the scope of the derived class, and thus the private member does not hide the base classes public member in the first place! Whether you use a local of the base or derived type, you're using the base classes member, because the derived classes member simply isn't in scope.

From the inside, the scope is different. Inside the derived class, the private member does hide the public member from the base class (and analogously with protected members, where derived classes also have the protected member in scope, while it still isn't in scope from the outside).

In fact, there's even an example of this very thing in the C# specification:

class Base { public static void F() {}  } 

class Derived: Base 
{ 
  new private static void F() {} // Hides Base.F in Derived only 
} 

class MoreDerived: Derived 
{ 
  static void G() { F(); } // Invokes Base.F
}

Since MoreDerived doesn't have the private Derived.F() method in scope, it uses the Base.F() method, which is in scope. But you would still get a compiler warning without the new modifier, because Derived.F() does hide Base.F() inside of the Derived class itself. In your case, the scope you're interested in isn't in a more derived class, but that's irrelevant for the private modifier, of course - it works the same way from any other class accessing Derived other than Derived itself.

It's all perfectly defined behaviour, and the AI "made" a mistake based on faulty assumptions - member hiding is not a property of the member, or the class, or anything like that. It's a property of scope. The compiler must warn you regardless, since there are a lot of potential scopes for the resolution to happen in (you wouldn't want to find out about ambiguities at point of use, would you?) - but it's just a warning. It was never anything other than a warning, as the specification clearly shows.

There's a good question about what the specification says about member hiding. But the framing the AI provides makes it a bit weird - it's kind of like "I made up a rule out of thin air, and when I came to test it, it didn't work. Why?" There's a deeper answer that I tried to provide, but there's also the more obvious answer of "Well, you just made up that rule. You shouldn't expect it to hold just because" :D

And hopefully that deeper answer helps you. It's probably not going to help the AI, unfortunately. If it didn't get the information from the very public C# specification, I suspect it's not going to get picked up here either - especially given that even on SO, a lot of answers are just wrong - that's why we have the voting and comments and sourcing and everything :D
